MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

AN APOLOGY IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR CONSTITUTIONAL COMPLIANCE: SUPREME COURT EXPOSES EXECUTIVE OVERREACH IN DELHI INTERNET BAN

The unfolding of this episode is a telling commentary on the precarious state of our constitutional governance. That the government, faced with the judicial scrutiny of an internet ban—a measure that strikes at the very root of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a)—has chosen to tender an unconditional apology, is a tacit admission of executive overreach.
 
However, an apology, however unconditional, cannot act as a panacea for a constitutional transgression. It is deeply concerning that an order imposing a blanket internet shutdown in the capital—crippling the flow of information and stifling dissent—was passed, seemingly without the application of mind, only to be withdrawn or apologized for once the judicial microscope was applied.
 
The Supreme Court is not merely a forum for dispute resolution; it is the ultimate sentinel on the qui vive, the guardian of the citizen's liberties against the might of the State. While the unconditional apology is noted, the Court must not allow this hasty retreat to bury the larger, grave questions of proportionality and legality under the guise of commotion.

The issuance of notice in the connected matters is a welcome step. The majesty of the Constitution demands that the executive be held accountable, for the rule of law cannot be reduced to a mere game of catch-me-if-you-can, where the State breaches fundamental rights and then seeks to absolve itself through a written apology.

UPSC Mains | Core Facts, Arguments & Insights:- 
Central Thesis: Internet Shutdowns are an extraordinary legal measure, permissible only under strict constitutional, statutory, and judicial safeguards, not as a routine administrative response.

Legal Framework: Internet suspension is governed by the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, replacing the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 and 2017 Rules.

Permissible Grounds: Shutdowns are allowed only in cases of Public Emergency or Public Safety, supported by written reasons, competent authority approval, and defined objectives.

Doctrine of Proportionality: Authorities must adopt the Least Restrictive Measure; blanket internet suspension should be the last resort, not the first response.

Supreme Court Doctrine: In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court held that internet access is intrinsically linked to Article 19(1)(a) (Freedom of Speech & Expression) and Article 19(1)(g) (Freedom of Trade & Profession).

Judicial Safeguards: Every shutdown order must be Reasoned, Time-Bound, Published, Subject to Review, and Open to Judicial Scrutiny; Indefinite Shutdowns are Unconstitutional.

Implementation Concern: Despite the new legal regime, some States reportedly continue relying on outdated legal provisions, raising concerns over procedural compliance and rule of law.

Global Position: India continues to record one of the world's highest numbers of internet shutdowns, making digital governance and rights protection key policy concerns.

Democratic Impact: Internet shutdowns affect Freedom of Expression, Digital Economy, Education, Emergency Services, Business Continuity, and Citizen Access to Information.

Policy Imperative: Strengthen Legal Accountability, Transparent Decision-Making, Periodic Review, Targeted Restrictions, and Digital Rights Protection while preserving Public Order.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

SpaceX, China, and the global rocket shortage 🚀

This video examines the mounting global rocket shortage and the geopolitical and economic factors driving a crisis in the space launch industry. 

The Genesis of China's Space Autonomy

The U.S. Wolf Amendment, passed 15 years ago, banned NASA from cooperating with China. Instead of limiting China, this forced the nation to build its own independent space infrastructure, including the Tiangong space station.

Today, China has achieved parity in areas like satellite navigation and remote sensing, and is aggressively developing reusable rocket technology to drive down launch costs.

__
The Launch Supply Crisis 

While the space industry appears to be in a "golden age" with record demand, there is a severe shortage of available rockets and launch providers.

Forecasts from the Commercial Space Federation suggest that over 7,000 satellites will be launched annually by the mid-2030s, far exceeding current capacity.

The industry faces a bottleneck:  satellite constellations are highly profitable, but the infrastructure to launch them—spaceports and rockets—is costly and lacks sufficient capital.

__
The SpaceX Bottleneck

SpaceX is shifting focus from its reliable Falcon 9 workhorse to the next-generation Starship.

This creates a conflict of interest:  SpaceX prioritizes launching its own Starlink satellites—which generate the bulk of the company's revenue—over servicing third-party contracts for companies like Amazon or the Pentagon.

__
Geopolitical Constraints and Market Alternatives

Western sanctions against Russia and the Wolf Amendment regarding China have restricted the global supply chain, limiting options for European and American operators.

With other nations like India and Japan struggling to scale their launch frequency, the market has become dangerously dependent on SpaceX.

Consequently, some policy analysts have speculated about the U.S. government potentially forcing SpaceX to continue the Falcon program or even nationalizing the company for national defense reasons.

Meanwhile, legacy players like ULA (a Boeing and Lockheed Martin venture) and Blue Origin are attempting to ramp up, but they have yet to match the operational pace of SpaceX.

__
The Future of Chinese Capacity

China’s ambitions remain aggressive, with permits recently filed for massive new constellations totaling 200,000 satellites.

While current ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulations) rules prevent Western firms from using Chinese launch services, the video warns that China may build excess capacity that becomes available to governments and companies outside the U.S. regulatory sphere

🚨 SHAME ON THE INDIAN GOVERNMENT! END ALL ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION! 🇮🇳🐕🐒💔

PM @narendramodi and the BJP government must answer: Why is India making animal experimentation easier to approve while other countries are moving towards animal-free science?

I UNEQUIVOCALLY CONDEMN ALL ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION. There is no such thing as morally acceptable or "humane" exploitation of an innocent animal.

🔴 1. INDIA'S ALARMING LABORATORY ANIMALS RULES, 2026

Under proposed Rule 11:

• Institutional ethics committees could approve "mild" and "moderate" experiments, including those involving dogs and monkeys, without referring them to the national CCSEA.

• Laboratories would gain greater authority over experimental approvals.

• Animal breeding, trading, confinement and experimentation would continue.

• There is NO binding roadmap to abolish animal experimentation.

Calling an experiment "mild" does not make it morally acceptable. Animals cannot consent to being experimented upon!

🔴 2. INDIA'S ANIMAL CRUELTY LAWS ARE A NATIONAL EMBARRASSMENT!

The British enacted animal cruelty legislation in India in 1890, 136 YEARS AGO!

Independent India replaced it with the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 — now 66 YEARS OLD!

And the maximum fine for a FIRST offence under Section 11?

A MEAGRE ₹50!

YES, FIFTY RUPEES IN 2026!

Repeat offences and other criminal provisions can attract stronger punishments, but how is a ₹50 first-offence fine remotely acceptable?

AND HERE IS THE BIGGEST IRONY!

Those entrusted with protecting animals should be urgently strengthening this outdated legislation, introducing meaningful punishments and preventing cruelty.

INSTEAD, THE MODI GOVERNMENT IS PROPOSING RULES THAT RAISE SERIOUS CONCERNS ABOUT WEAKENED NATIONAL OVERSIGHT OF ANIMAL EXPERIMENTS!

Animals need protection from experimentation, NOT a more convenient system for approving it!

🇺🇸 3. MEANWHILE, THE UNITED STATES IS MOVING IN ANOTHER DIRECTION!

• Congresswoman Nancy Mace introduced the PUPPS Act in September 2026 to prohibit breeding dogs for research.
https://t.co/HDQm0ugGYo

• Bipartisan lawmakers proposed restricting federal funding for experiments involving live dogs and cats.
https://t.co/b1nn6Hm0wt

• Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced initiatives to reduce animal testing and expand human-based research.
https://t.co/LltVNUWKkt

• The US FDA announced plans to phase out animal-testing requirements for certain medicines.

The US has not banned all animal testing, but these developments demonstrate growing efforts to replace it.

🌍 4. OTHER COUNTRIES ARE ALREADY RESTRICTING ANIMAL TESTING!

🇪🇺 EU: Animal testing for cosmetics is banned.

🇨🇦 CANADA: Cosmetic animal testing is prohibited.

🇬🇧 UK: Animal testing for cosmetics is banned.

🇦🇺 AUSTRALIA: Restrictions on new animal-testing data for cosmetic ingredients.

These are not universal bans, but they show that animal testing can be prohibited by law.

WHY SHOULD INDIA NOT AIM TO ABOLISH ALL ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION?

🔴 5. STOP CALLING ANIMAL EXPERIMENTATION "HUMANE"!

A larger cage is still a cage.

A supposedly "mild" experiment is still an experiment imposed on an animal without consent.

Reducing suffering is NOT the same as ending exploitation.

Dogs, monkeys, rabbits, mice and countless other animals experience fear, distress and pain.

THEY ARE NOT DISPOSABLE LABORATORY EQUIPMENT!

🔴 6. MY DEMANDS ARE CLEAR!

• Withdraw provisions weakening national oversight.
• Establish a legally binding roadmap to END ALL animal experimentation.
• End breeding and trading animals for laboratory research.
• Overhaul India's 66-year-old animal cruelty legislation.
• Replace absurdly inadequate penalties with meaningful punishments.
• Invest in organ-on-chip technology, human-cell models and animal-free scientific research.
• Recognise animals as sentient beings deserving protection, not objects for human exploitation.

text:
The United States is not a surveillance state. Especially not Florida. Police do not need the power of god. They do not need AI cameras watching our every move. To the officers and FLOCK advocates saying “FLOCK cameras only capture license plates”, it doesn’t matter what they capture right now, today. What matters is the implication. What matters is that we, the people of the United States, draw a line here and now to prevent the technology from developing and being weaponized against us. 

If you’ve read a history book, one common theme you find again and again is that once lost, rights are only regained through war. Saying, “yes, we don’t mind if AI integrated cameras photograph our license plates and track our movement through the state” now makes it only another small step a couple years down the line to say, “yes, we don’t mind if AI integrated, cameras with facial recognition are set up every 50’ in our neighborhoods to track our movement from the moment we step out of our doors in the morning until we come home.” 

You may say, “that’s a stretch!” And to that I’d say, 10 years ago you would’ve called it outlandish that the police would be tracking you as you drive through your town. 

And to those of you who say, “if you don’t have anything to hide, you should have nothing to worry about!” 

Sure, let’s explore that. Let’s say we have another “global pandemic” 

Nation wide mandate, ‘No gatherings of more than 10 people’ how many millions of Americans gathered for church anyway? Had a baby shower? A Sunday family dinner? With this kind of technology implemented across the country, you would see door to door arrests. The burden of proof, taken care of before the trial. You can go to court as a formality, try to have your attorney fight for you, at that point it’s just a formality. 

Desantis has done the right thing and shut the FLOCK program down. But this won’t be the last we see of FLOCK as Floridians. There were 2 republicans candidates on the ballot who opposed FLOCK. Paul Renner and James Fishback. Byron Donalds, a man who is very pro FLOCK won the nomination. 

Here are a list of countries who use a similar system to mass surveil their citizens: 

- China
- Russia 
- United Kingdom 
- France 
- United Arab Emirates 
- Canada 
- Germany 
- Japan 
- India 

What do each one of these countries have in common? In every single country listed above, a citizen can be arrested, prosecuted, and imprisoned for speech alone. In many of these countries criticizing the government is criminal. 

Freedom is rarely taken in a single stroke; it is surrendered inch by inch, until nothing remains but the memory of liberty.

America is one of the last truly free places on this planet. That freedom is fragile. 

“An uninformed electorate is a threat to a free republic.
Inform yourself. Think critically. Vote accordingly.” -me

text:
Tracket Daily · India Q2 FY27 results & market news · 19 Oct 2026 (Hindi video) #Q2FY27

Part 1: 11 Indian companies: quarterly results and earnings calls, by sector, with the best results of each industry this season.

Part 2: 3 Indian companies' business updates, plus orders, deals and policy, by sector.

STRONG: #HFCL
QUALITY: #BAJFINANCE #ULTRACEMCO #HINDZINC #UNIONBANK #POLYCAB #ICICIGI
MIXED: #LTTS #TATVA #TATATECH
WEAK: #WAAREERTL

PART 1 · EARNINGS & RESULTS

━━ Financial Services ━━

#BAJFINANCE · QUALITY results · Score 7/10

Consolidated PAT ₹6,367 Cr (+29% YoY, +4.7% QoQ) on AUM of ₹5.85 lakh Cr (+26% YoY, +6.9% QoQ); credit cost 1.56% vs 1.88% a year ago

Bajaj Finance is still growing loans and profit at close to 30% a year with bad loans under control, but it now wants a big dose of fresh capital and a pocket of gold loans needs watching.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 (festive Oct–Dec 2026 quarter) results, date not yet announced: whether the ₹1,047 Cr gold-loan Stage 2 bump unwinds and credit cost stays near 1.3% before overlays. Alongside that, the shareholder vote and final terms of the up to ₹17,500 Cr equity raise.

#UNIONBANK · QUALITY results · Score 6/10

Net profit ₹5,537 Cr, +30.3% YoY and +3.8% QoQ; NII ₹10,583 Cr, +20.1% YoY and +5.4% QoQ, with loans +18.5% YoY and gross NPA down to 2.42%.

Union Bank is lending much more and earning more on it with fewer bad loans, but its deposits are not keeping pace, so funding that growth is the next test.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 results (date not yet announced): whether deposit growth catches up with loans so the CD ratio eases from 88% without NIM slipping below 2.86%, and how much of the roughly ₹6,000 Cr ECL provision gets built before April 2027.

#ICICIGI · QUALITY results · Score 5/10

Q2 FY27 PAT ₹946 cr, up 15.5% YoY and 2.3x QoQ (Q1 base hit by one-offs); revenue ₹6,652 cr, +17.7% YoY, +11.8% QoQ.

ICICI Lombard bounced back from a one-off-hit June quarter with profit up about 15% on last year, but half-year profit is still below last year's, so the recovery needs another quarter to prove itself.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 results (likely mid-January 2027 going by the July and October call dates; date not announced): whether the combined ratio holds at or below Q2's 104.5% with no new Supreme Court-related reserve, and whether the 12–15% motor third-party premium revision is notified. Nearer term, the 23 October 2026 investor meeting in Mumbai (company says no new price-sensitive information will be shared).

Strongest in Financial Services: SGFIN

SG Finserve's STRONG results, score 7, are the sector's highest grade and the freshest full quarterly numbers: Q2 FY27 PAT up 106% YoY to ₹58.5 Cr on a loan book up 98% to ₹5,694 Cr, with NPAs still nil. Today's best, Bajaj Finance, is a grade lower at QUALITY 7.

━━ Capital Goods ━━

#WAAREERTL · WEAK results · Score 5/10

Q2 FY27 revenue ₹1,057.8 cr, +36.5% YoY and +14.5% QoQ, all of it from the APSPL acquisition; PAT ₹81.5 cr, -30.0% YoY and -31.5% QoQ (owners' share ₹73.9 cr, -36.5% YoY) as EBITDA margin fell to 15.1% from 20.4% and core solar EPC revenue dropped 42% YoY.

Revenue grew only because of the transmission business Waaree RTL acquired in June; its own solar work shrank by about 42% and profit fell 30%, though a ₹5,500+ cr order book gives it room to recover.

Watch next: Whether solar EPC revenue recovers from ₹445 cr toward its earlier ₹770-800 cr quarterly level in Q3 FY27 (results expected around January 2027), and management's explanation for the Q2 drop on the Q2 FY27 earnings call (date not in the pack).

#POLYCAB · QUALITY results · Score 5/10

Q2 FY27: revenue ₹9,899 Cr (+53% YoY, +21% QoQ), record PAT ₹990 Cr (+43% YoY, +24% QoQ); EBITDA margin 14.4%, up 0.5 pp QoQ but down 1.4 pp YoY

Polycab's profit hit a record and grew over 40%, but much of the 53% sales jump came from pricier copper, so the real test is whether it sells more cable, not just costlier cable.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 results (due around January 2027; date not in the pack): wires-and-cables volume growth, as opposed to copper-driven price growth, and whether EBITDA margin holds near 14%.

Strongest in Capital Goods: SAMBHV

Sambhv Steel Tubes holds the sector's highest grade and score, STRONG with 7: record Q2 volume of 1.23 lakh tonnes, up 24% YoY and 14% QoQ, with value-added products at 93% of the mix. Today's Polycab (QUALITY 5) and Waaree RTL (WEAK 5) rank below it.

━━ Information Technology ━━

#LTTS · MIXED results · Score 6/10

Q2 FY27 revenue ₹3,040 Cr, +3.4% QoQ and +12.1% YoY (constant currency +2.7% QoQ, +4.8% YoY); EBIT margin 16.3% (+60 bps QoQ, +220 bps YoY); continuing net profit ₹380 Cr, +7.9% QoQ and +19.7% YoY. Reported ₹548 Cr (+66.8% YoY) includes a ₹165 Cr one-time gain.

LTTS is earning noticeably more profit on each rupee of work and winning bigger AI-related contracts, but its dollar sales are still growing only about 5% a year, and much of the headline 67% profit jump is a one-time gain from selling a business.

Watch next: Whether the Tech segment returns to growth and constant-currency revenue growth accelerates beyond Q2's 2.7% QoQ, as management promised for H2 — next check is the Q3 FY27 results, likely mid-January 2027 (last year's Q3 call was on 17 Jan 2026).

#TATATECH · MIXED results · Score 4/10

Q2 FY27: revenue ₹1,699 Cr (+28.4% YoY, +2.1% QoQ), PAT ₹171 Cr (+3.6% YoY, -5.2% QoQ); operating EBITDA margin flat at 16.1%; FY27 double-digit growth guidance maintained on the call.

Tata Technologies is winning more engineering work and its sales jumped 28% in a year, but acquisition costs and a soft German business meant profit barely grew, so earnings are lagging the sales growth for now.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 results and call (around January 2027; date not in the pack): whether operating EBITDA margin finally moves above 16.1% as promised, whether Services growth speeds up from ~4% QoQ as the large deals ramp, and the size of any Germany restructuring cost.

Strongest in Information Technology: HCLTECH

HCL Technologies' QUALITY results, score 7, still lead the sector: record PAT of ₹5,132 Cr (+21.2% YoY), EBIT margin up to 18.2%, new bookings of $3,258 mn (+27% YoY) and an FY27 guidance floor raised to 2.5%. Today's LTTS and Tata Technologies are both MIXED.

━━ Chemicals ━━

#TATVA · MIXED results · Score 6/10

Record revenue of ₹217 Cr, +76% YoY and +30% QoQ; PAT ₹21.5 Cr, +116% YoY and +34% QoQ; but EBITDA margin slipped to 18.7%, below the 20–22% FY27 guidance.

Tatva Chintan's sales are booming on demand for its emission-control chemical, but costlier solvents and shipping kept margins below what management promised, and its factories are nearly full until a new plant arrives in 2028.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 results (Oct–Dec 2026 quarter; date not yet announced): whether EBITDA margin returns to the 20–22% guided band as management expects solvent and freight costs to normalise within Q3, and whether revenue holds near Q2's ₹217 Cr with plants close to full.

Strongest in Chemicals: TATVA

Tatva Chintan's MIXED results, score 6, are the best in a sector where every name is MIXED: record revenue of ₹217 Cr (+76% YoY) and clean PAT of ₹21.5 Cr (+116% YoY), though its 18.7% EBITDA margin is below the 20–22% guidance.

━━ Construction Materials ━━

#ULTRACEMCO · QUALITY results · Score 6/10

Q2 FY27: revenue ₹23,295 Cr (+18.8% YoY, -5.5% QoQ), operating EBITDA ₹3,721 Cr (+20.3% YoY, -25.8% QoQ), PAT ₹1,501 Cr (+21.3% YoY, -42.3% QoQ) on 12.9% volume growth; EBITDA per tonne ₹974, up ₹60 YoY.

India's biggest cement maker is selling about 13% more cement than a year ago and earning more per tonne, but costly fuel made the monsoon quarter thin and a big dividend plus expansion spending has pushed its debt up.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 (Oct–Dec 2026) results: whether operating EBITDA per tonne climbs back from ₹974 toward Q1's ₹1,200-plus as fuel costs ease and peak-season volumes arrive, and whether net debt starts falling from ₹23,536 Cr toward the below-1x EBITDA promise; result date not in the pack.

Strongest in Construction Materials: ULTRACEMCO

UltraTech's QUALITY results, score 6, are the only grade above MIXED in the sector: volume up 12.9% to 38.2 million tonnes and EBITDA of ₹974 a tonne against India Cements' ₹510, on 210.1 mtpa of capacity.

━━ Metals & Mining ━━

#HINDZINC · QUALITY results · Score 6/10

Record Q2 FY27: revenue ₹15,093 Cr (+77% YoY, +10% QoQ), EBITDA ₹9,285 Cr at a 62% margin (+108% YoY, +15% QoQ), net profit ₹6,412 Cr (+142% YoY, +17% QoQ).

Hindustan Zinc just had its most profitable quarter ever, mostly because zinc and silver prices and a weaker rupee went its way, though it also produced more silver and cut its costs.

Watch next: Q3 FY27 (Oct–Dec 2026) production: refined metal needs to step up to ~288 KT a quarter (from 264 KT) and silver to ~180 t to meet the FY27 guide of 1.1 MT and ~680 t, alongside the board decision on the 600+ KT smelter expansion promised by end-December 2026.

Strongest in Metals & Mining: HINDZINC

Hindustan Zinc's QUALITY results, score 6, top Vedanta Aluminium's QUALITY 5 and the MIXED rest: record net profit of ₹6,412 Cr (+142% YoY) at a 62% EBITDA margin, record refined metal of 264 KT and about ₹11,268 Cr more cash and investments than borrowings.

━━ Telecommunication ━━

#HFCL · STRONG results · Score 6/10

Q2 FY27 consolidated revenue ₹2,542 Cr (+144% YoY, +33% QoQ), EBITDA ₹658 Cr at a 25.9% margin, net profit ₹394 Cr (+448% YoY, +60% QoQ); order book ₹28,911 Cr and FY27 growth guidance raised to at least 80%.

HFCL just posted its best quarter ever as fibre for AI data centres and exports drove sales and margins sharply higher, but its defence push and old contracting arm still lag.

Watch next: Next quarterly results (Q3 FY27, date not yet announced): whether revenue holds at or above ~₹2,230 Cr a quarter, the pace the at-least-80% FY27 guide needs, and whether defence revenue finally scales toward the ~₹500 Cr aspiration.

Strongest in Telecommunication: HFCL

HFCL's STRONG results, score 6, outrank RailTel's MIXED 4: revenue up 144% YoY to ₹2,542 Cr and net profit up 448% to ₹394 Cr at a 25.9% EBITDA margin, backed by a ₹28,911 Cr order book and FY27 growth guidance raised to at least 80%.

PART 2 · NEWS & BUSINESS UPDATES

━━ Chemicals ━━

#SILKFLEX

Commercial production of textile garment printing inks started at Vadodara on 19 Oct 2026 on two 2 MT vessels, so 4 MT a day per shift. The update has no revenue or profit figures; the last reported half (H2 FY26) had revenue of ₹72.6 Cr and PAT of ₹8.7 Cr, against ₹37.6 Cr and ₹3.4 Cr in H1 FY26.

Silkflex has started making its own garment-printing inks, a quick but small step towards the higher-margin factory model it promised; the half-year numbers in November will show whether it is paying off.

Watch next: H1 FY27 (Apr–Sep 2026) results, due by mid-November 2026 under the 45-day deadline. Check revenue against ₹37.6 Cr a year ago, plant utilisation (about 60% at the last call), EBITDA margin against the 20–25% goal, and finance cost now that the term-loan moratorium has ended.

━━ Construction ━━

#POWERMECH

Vedanta Aluminium awards Power Mech a ₹327 Cr, 4-year O&M contract (~₹82 Cr a year, est., ~10% of O&M backlog); last reported Q1 FY27 revenue ₹1,624 Cr, +25.5% YoY, −23.1% QoQ

Power Mech won a steady four-year job running a Vedanta power plant, worth about ₹327 crore. That is good recurring income but small next to the real question: whether its orders and margins catch up with management's promises this year.

Watch next: Q2 FY27 results (date not in the pack): whether the EBITDA margin climbs from Q1's 10.8% toward the 12.5% FY27 guide, and how far H1 order inflow has reached against the ₹12,000 Cr goal. After that, the washery hot commissioning at the second mine, guided for November–December 2026.

━━ Consumer Services ━━

#IMAGICAA

Q2 FY27 footfalls about 2.1 lakh, down 6% YoY (heavy rain in July–August) and down ~82% QoQ from the 11.54 lakh summer peak; ₹248 Cr Novotel sale agreed and ₹129.45 Cr warrant balance received.

Heavy monsoon rain meant about 6% fewer visitors at Imagicaa's parks this quarter, but the company is raising cash through a ₹248 Cr sale of its hotel and by collecting ₹129 Cr from investors to fund new water parks and indoor play centres that depend less on the weather.

Watch next: Q2 FY27 results (date not in the pack): the size of the monsoon-quarter loss against ₹38.9 Cr a year ago and how Novotel is accounted for; then the Hyderabad Hello Park opening in Q3 FY27 (Oct–Dec 2026) and completion of the Juniper Hotels deal.

Hey there #Uranium peeps!👋 When market noise and a severe unwarranted U #stocks sell-off📉 have investors questioning their investment thesis💰⚛️⛽️🐂😟 even as they see a non-stop torrent of bullish news about the biggest boom in #Nuclear power since the 1980s🌏⏫⚛️🏗️👷 while the production of the required uranium fuel supply continues to struggle⛏️🏭🧑‍🏭🐌 it's clearly time to review the first principles that are creating the set-up for what may be the most spectacular commodity bull run in history.🚀🌜🌟

🧑‍🏫Up until a few short years ago at the UN's COP28 Climate Change Conference in December 2023, when Nuclear power was formally recognized for the very first time in a UN climate summit agreement as a key solution to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and reach net-zero by 2050, nations around the world were planning to gradually phase out their use of Nuclear power.☹️

Many countries were planning to close reactors at the end of their licensed operating life or, like Germany, aggressively shut them down for no rational reason with failed expectations of running a modern industrial economy on intermittent wind & solar power. 🤪

However, the outlook for Nuclear power changed almost overnight!😃 38 nations have now signed on to a pledge to TRIPLE global Nuclear power capacity by 2050, working together to develop an achievable plan to expand Nuclear from around 400 Gigawatts to 1,200 Gigawatts over the next 25 years.3⃣✖️⚛️🏗️👷🌏  

Countries like South Korea, for example, have completely reversed course from a planned total phase-out to a full-on Nuclear Renaissance, discarding shutdown plans in favour of life-extending existing reactors, building new ones and embracing the move towards mass-produced, factory built Small Modular Reactors (SMR) as the ultimate solution to provide both 24/7 carbon-free electricity and industrial heat which can be co-located with large scale manufacturing and processing plants.⚡️⚛️🏭🔥  

SMRs provide the flexibility of being grid-connected or operating standalone to power remote communities, industry, mines and power-hungry data centers. Nuclear's 'Henry Ford moment' approaches!⚛️🏭🧑‍🏭

All around the world now we are seeing country after country shelving their phase-out plans and instead commit to upgrading & extending their Nuclear power plants to operate for as long as 100 years, more than double their initial design life of 40 years!🧓

🇨🇳China has taken the lead in developing the reactor supply chains and workforce needed to build a large fleet of identical reactors in cookie-cutter fashion, with build times now dropping to just over 5 years per reactor, today constructing 38 new reactors all at the same time, which is nearly half of the record 80 reactors now under construction worldwide.😲

🇮🇳India has been watching China's huge expansion program with envy and have now launched their own Nuclear resurgence with a plan in motion to increase capacity 12-fold to 100 Gigawatts by 2047 with a mix of indigenous designed reactors and SMRs. The growth trajectory for Nuclear power is truly mind-blowing!🤯

But the tailwinds for Nuclear power and uranium demand continue to mount!🌀⚛️🌊🏄

🇷🇺Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine caused many European and western nations to question the state of their energy security and their overreliance on Russian uranium, oil & gas supplies.😨  Many have now pivoted away from Russia, have moved to expand the use of Nuclear power for stable 24/7 energy security, and in the US & Europe invest in strategic expansion of uranium conversion & enrichment to replace what has for decades been provided by Russia. The US has relied on Russia to supply around 20% of its enriched uranium fuel. That dependence, by law, stops at the end of 2027.

Then Artificial Intelligence stepped up to the plate.⚾️🤖 AI computer systems cannot operate on intermittent power!  They need guaranteed 24/7 "always on" electricity for their data centers and associated cooling systems.  Big tech companies are also cognizant of the need to avoid real or perceived increases in greenhouse gases and air pollution stemming from this AI revolution, so are making major investments and big bets on clean 24/7 carbon-free Nuclear as their best long-term power source, with natgas as a temporary bridge. Over the past year we've seen a growing list of big tech companies announce Nuclear power purchase agreements and plans to fund reactor uprates and new builds.  This added tailwind seemed to come out of nowhere, but that's all it is - an add-on to an already emerging global Nuclear Renaissance!🌀🌊🏄

🪖Then came Trump's US war on Iran, upending global oil, gas, sulphur, and other vital commodity markets, sending the world into another energy crisis. The war on Iran has lit yet another fire under the global push to get off fossil fuels and achieve energy security by embracing safe 24/7 reliable carbon-free power for both clean electricity and emissions-free industrial heat.  Many nations are taking a second look at Nuclear power, which, compared to power generation with diesel oil & natgas, is nearly immune to short term fuel supply disruptions.  Nuclear reactors have several years of uranium fuel on-site, and the cost of that fuel is small compared to overall operating costs.

Just as happened in the 1970s, the 2026 Iran War has triggered a global energy crisis that is driving an even more powerful move to embrace and expand the use of Nuclear power to provide long-term energy security.🔒⚛️🏗️👷

Now comes the other side of the equation: uranium supply.⛏️⛽️

The Uranium mining industry never saw all these tailwinds for Nuclear energy on the horizon.  Investment in new mines was delayed or outright cancelled. Mines were shut down and put into care & maintenance as the price of uranium bottomed to under $18 in 2016. Investment dried up and continues to be insufficient to bring enough new supply online.  Shuttered mines have slowly been restarting, with never-ending challenges causing setback after setback, but very little new greenfield mine construction is taking place so far.🦥

As Uranium sector investing guru Mike Alkin has been saying for years, supply/demand is really just a math problem.🧮

China is accelerating its Nuclear expansion by cutting the reactor build time down to 5 years per reactor, building 38 reactors at the same time, but it takes on average about 15 to 20 years to bring a new uranium mine into production to supply the required fuel!😲

A lack of sufficient investment in exploration & development, delayed financing & construction of new mines, soaring operating costs & borrowing rates, and a long period of inventory drawdown by Nuclear utilities while exercising flexing options in existing supply contracts instead of investing in building new mines, has led to a deep structural supply deficit that is expected to continue to grow in the decade ahead.↕️🗜️

The stage is set🎭 and Cameco's Grant Isaac told us on the company's Q2 Results Conference Call precisely why we are now on the cusp of a coming Uranium bull market for the history books!⚛️⛏️🐂🚀🌜 On the call Grant said:

"I think what the most notable point to make is we are still not at replacement rate demand across the industry.  We still don't have utilities coming forward and collectively buying at a volume that replaces what they consume under existing contracts!  And yet we find ourselves back into a mid-90s long-term uranium price on its way to 3 digits likely.  And that's in the absence of replacement rate demand.  And as I remind folks, we've never been at this kind of uranium price [$97] on the front end of a uranium contracting cycle. We've only ever found ourselves at these prices on the back end."

He reminded us of 2 important factors:

1. Nuclear utilities normally sign a series of 4 different contracts to order reactor fuel🧾✍️⚛️🏭 starting with the fabrication of fuel assemblies filled with enriched uranium to be loaded into reactors 1⃣  then working backwards thru SWU for enrichment of UF6 2⃣  and Conversion of drummed U3O8 into UF6 3⃣  then finally, last of all, they sign contracts with miners to supply the required drums of mined U3O8 yellow cake 4⃣ the last link in the contracts chain.🛢️☢️🔗

⚠️ Prices for Conversion and enrichment SWU have already skyrocketed 200-300% to all-time highs, indicating that utilities have been squeezing the conversion & enrichment markets signing a large volume of new service contracts🗜️🛒 but they haven't yet signed sufficient contracts for the mined U3O8 that must be converted & enriched!🚨

This is most evident by looking at long-term contracting volumes.📊 For the past 13 years, utilities on average globally have only been signing uranium supply contracts for little more than half the volume of uranium they have been consuming in reactors each year!  Contracting has been far below what is referred to as "replacement rate" due to utilities being focused primarily on securing the most important contracts for fabrication, SWU and Conversion, putting off signing contracts for mined U3O8 until the last minute.😴 Hence, there is a massive wave of contracting volume yet to arrive at mined U3O8, the last domino to fall in the contracts chain.🌊🛢️☢️🛒
 
2. Grant also reminded investors that the published long-term Uranium price has now reached a new all-time record high of $97/lb, higher than the $95 peak during the last 2006/2007 bull market, but replacement rate contracting by utilities hasn't even started yet! 😲

The coming "replacement rate" contracting cycle is going to start off at a higher long-term price than was ever achieved at the back-end months of the last uranium bull market!

Once fuel buyers jump back into signing a high volume of new U3O8 supply contracts, the Long-term and Spot prices will go far far higher from today's already elevated base prices!⏫💲

In the first 3 years of the last Uranium bull market the long-term price rose from ~$25 in 2005 to a peak of $95 in 2007/2008, a near 4-fold price jump.  Meanwhile, Spot U3O8 went from ~$20 to a peak of $136 in 2007, a near 7-fold price run!

But wait!✋ There's more... 😄
As Grant said, 'replacement rate' only deals with replacing the uranium fuel that is being consumed by today's operating reactors under existing contracts signed years ago!🌎⚛️⛽️  

Additional demand coming from ~80 new reactors under construction today (which nominally load 3 years worth of uranium fuel at start-up), shuttered plants like Palisades, Three Mile Island, Duane Arnold and others worldwide being restarted, as well as the growing number of reactors now unexpectedly receiving new multi-decade life extensions, will drive the required amount of fuel purchasing to a level far above today's replacement rate in order to secure the much higher quantities of fuel that will be required⬆️🛢️☢️🛒😊 which Bloomberg recently calculated to be a +44% increase of 163 Gigawatts😲 adding around 80 Million lbs PER YEAR of new uranium demand by 2036!😲 

In spite of this irrational U sector pullback, VERY exciting times are still ahead for U!😃

IMHO, this recent deep and unwarranted sell-off is, as Lobo Tiggre puts it, a "huge mistake" by investors, especially those with tunnel vision looking only at the small AI portion of a much bigger global Nuclear expansion vs lagging uranium supply situation.🙈  If U have the cash to deploy, now is certainly an opportune time to consider putting that cash to work ahead of the imminent coming wave of replacement-rate contracting that will drive U prices far higher.🌊🏄

Good luck with your research & investments!☘️🌈💰It's your money... invest it wisely!🦉🤠🐂

text:
Kolar, INO, and why India needs big experiments

In 1965, a TIFR-led team caught neutrinos made in Earth's own atmosphere, 2.3 km down the Kolar Gold Fields. It was one of the first two detections of atmospheric neutrinos anywhere in the world. A team in a South African mine got there the same summer.

Sixty-one years later, India has no large neutrino detector.

I asked Prof. Basudeb Dasgupta of TIFR Mumbai @thebdasgupta  what the India-based Neutrino Observatory, INO, was meant to find.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜𝗡𝗢 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿

Cosmic rays hit the top of our atmosphere all the time. The particle showers they set off make neutrinos, called atmospheric neutrinos. They rain down from every direction and pass straight through the Earth as if it were not there.

INO was designed to catch them in a cavern under a mountain. Rock blocks almost everything else, but not neutrinos.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱

Neutrinos come in three mass states. Experiments have measured the gaps between those masses, but not their order. Either two are light and one is heavy ("normal ordering"), or one is light and two are heavy ("inverted ordering").

As Basu puts it: both are theoretically possible, but nature will choose one. INO would have helped us find out which.

It is not a trivia question. The ordering changes:
• what searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay should expect (is the neutrino its own antiparticle?)
• what the neutrino burst from an exploding star should look like in our detectors
• how small the total mass of neutrinos is allowed to be

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗜𝗡𝗢

• 2010–11: the site moves to the Bodi West Hills in Theni, Tamil Nadu. Forest clearance comes in October 2010, environmental clearance in June 2011.
• Jan 2015: the Union Cabinet approves INO at about ₹1,583 crore. The plan is a 50,000-tonne magnetised iron detector under more than a kilometre of rock. Its magnet could tell neutrinos from antineutrinos.
• 2015: the clearance is challenged at the National Green Tribunal, and the Madras High Court's Madurai bench rules that no work can start until the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board consents.
• 2017–18: the tribunal suspends the clearance; a fresh one is granted in March 2018 and the tribunal upholds it. The fight moves to the Supreme Court.
• 2022: Tamil Nadu tells the Supreme Court it will not allow construction, because the site sits in the Mathikettan–Periyar tiger corridor.
• 2026: still not built. INO's 85-tonne prototype, mini-ICAL, was switched on in Madurai in 2018.

Meanwhile, China's JUNO broke ground the same month INO was approved, and it has been taking data since August 2025. It is a different kind of detector: it watches neutrinos from nuclear reactors in a tank of liquid scintillator. But it is chasing the same question.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀

This one is not a regular podcast episode. It is a class, in Hindi. Basu explains neutrinos from zero, and I ask the questions people are too shy to ask in a classroom:

• Why physics needed the neutrino in the first place
• How a particle "impossible to catch" was caught
• A one-cubic-kilometre telescope in the South Pole ice: IceCube, which won Francis Halzen this year's Nobel Prize in Physics
• Kolar, INO, and why India needs big experiments

Basu is a theoretical physicist at TIFR who works on neutrinos from exploding stars and on dark matter. He won the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in 2022.

Images: NASA; ESO/H.H. Heyer (CC BY 4.0).

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in
